opus-5.5.text:
I think game data is one of the most underrated resources we have, and the reason has to do with what generalization actually requires.

Most of what today's large models learn from is text, and text is a compressed, after-the-fact description of the world. Someone did something, observed the result, and then wrote it down. What's missing is the loop itself: the action, the consequence, the adjustment. Games are basically millions of those loops, recorded at very high density. A player sees a state, takes an action, the environment responds, and the player updates. That's the raw material of agency, not just knowledge.

So when I think about an "ultimate" foundation model, I don't think of it only as something that knows a lot. I think of it as something that can act sensibly in situations it has never seen. For that you need exposure to enormous diversity of environments with consistent internal rules. Games give you exactly that. Every game is its own little universe with its own physics, economy, social norms, and goals. If a model can infer the rules of a new game quickly from a few interactions, that's a very good proxy for the kind of generalization we care about in the real world.

There are maybe three layers to it.

The first is perception and physics. Games, especially 3D ones, teach spatial reasoning, object permanence, cause and effect, and how things move and collide. It's not perfect physics, but it's structured and controllable, and you can generate as much as you want.

The second is decision-making over long horizons. Strategy games, open-world games, and RPGs involve planning across hours, managing resources, and trading short-term against long-term reward. That's very hard to learn from static text, because text rarely shows you the full trajectory, especially the failures.

The third, which I find most interesting, is the social and human layer. Multiplayer games contain cooperation, competition, deception, negotiation, and teamwork, all grounded in real outcomes. You see how humans actually behave when something is at stake, not how they say they would behave.

I should be honest about the limitations too. Game data has strong biases: the worlds are designed to be fun, which means they're often more forgiving or more legible than reality. And the action spaces are usually discrete and narrow. So I don't think game data alone gets you there. But as a bridge between pure language models and embodied agents in the real world, I think it's essential. It's where a model can practice being an agent cheaply and safely, with millions of lives to spend, before it ever touches a robot or a real-world decision.

If I had to put it in one sentence: text teaches a model what the world is like, but games can teach it how to live in a world it doesn't fully understand yet. And that second ability is really what generalization means.

fable-5.1.text:
I think game data is one of the most underrated pieces of this puzzle, and I'll try to explain why from the perspective of what a foundation model actually needs to learn.

Right now, most of what a model sees is text, images, maybe video. All of that is observational. The model watches the world go by, but it never acts in it. It never makes a choice and then sees the consequence of that choice. And I think that gap, between observing and acting, is one of the biggest things standing between where we are and a genuinely general model.

Games close that gap. A game is a world with rules, with physics of some kind, with other agents, and most importantly with feedback. You do something, the world responds. You plan over ten steps, and you find out whether the plan worked. That's not just more data, it's a different kind of data. It teaches causality, long-horizon planning, exploration, dealing with uncertainty, and all the things that are very hard to extract from a static corpus.

The other thing I'd point out is diversity. Every game is essentially a small, self-contained universe with its own rules. A strategy game, a physics puzzle, an open-world game, a social deduction game, they each stress different capabilities. If you train across thousands of these worlds, you're forcing the model to learn how to pick up new rules quickly, instead of memorizing one environment. That's generalization in the most literal sense: adapt to a world you haven't seen before.

And then there's the practical argument. Games are cheap to generate at scale, they're safe to fail in, and the reward signal is usually clear. If I want a model to learn something about embodied interaction without putting a robot in a kitchen a million times, games are the closest proxy we have. I think of them as a kind of simulator for agency.

So when people ask what the ultimate foundation model looks like, my answer is that it can't just be a very good reader. It has to be something that has acted, has made mistakes, and has learned from consequences. Games are where we can give it that experience today.

astra-6.text:
I think game data can contribute something important: experience with actions and their consequences. A model has to understand a situation, make a decision, see what changes, and adjust. That gives it a way to learn planning and decision-making, alongside recognizing patterns.

But being very good at one game isn’t necessarily generalization. The interesting question is whether the model can enter a new game, infer its rules, and reuse what it learned elsewhere. Can it adapt when the objectives change, or when a familiar strategy stops working? You’d want diverse games and environments to encourage that.

For an ultimate foundation model, I’d see game data as one part of the training experience. Games provide a setting for learning through interaction, but their rules and rewards are often clearer than those of the real world. The real test is whether the capabilities learned there transfer beyond those environments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think game data is valuable because games let you connect perception, action, and consequences. You’re not just learning what a scene looks like; you’re learning what you can do in that scene, how the world changes, and whether your strategy works over time.

That creates an opportunity to learn planning, exploration, and adaptation. You can vary the rules, the environments, and the goals, then ask whether the model can handle a situation it hasn’t seen before. Does it pick up the underlying structure, or has it just memorized a successful sequence of actions?

But being good at games doesn’t automatically mean you generalize to the real world. Games have their own assumptions and shortcuts. For an ultimate foundation model, I would see game data as one part of the training mix—a way to develop and test interactive capabilities, alongside other kinds of experience. The important question is whether what it learns transfers beyond the game.
